mcqs.q: Pharmacokinetics is best defined as:
opts: What the body does to the drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion)
What the drug does to the body
The chemical synthesis of a drug
mcqs.explain: Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug (ADME); pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body.

mcqs.q: Which route is ENTERAL?
mcqs.explain: Enteral routes use the GI tract (oral, sublingual, buccal, rectal); IV, IM and inhalation are parenteral.

mcqs.q: The route preferred in EMERGENCIES, and the only one with 100% bioavailability, is:
mcqs.explain: IV is preferred in emergencies and is 100% bioavailable because the drug enters the blood directly.

mcqs.q: A key advantage of the SUBLINGUAL route is that it:
opts: Gives excellent absorption while avoiding gastric acidity and first-pass metabolism
Is the slowest of all routes
Requires the patient to be unconscious
Delivers the drug to the skin
mcqs.explain: Sublingual absorption is rapid and bypasses gastric acid and hepatic first-pass metabolism.

mcqs.q: The RECTAL route is mainly reserved for:
mcqs.explain: Rectal (PR) administration is reserved for unconscious or vomiting patients.

mcqs.q: Which route provides the MOST RAPID absorption via a large surface area?
mcqs.explain: Inhalation gives very rapid absorption through the large alveolar surface of the lungs.

mcqs.q: The four processes of pharmacokinetics (ADME) are:
mcqs.explain: ADME = Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism and Excretion.

mcqs.q: Absorption is the process of a drug moving:
opts: From the administration site into the systemic circulation
mcqs.explain: Absorption is movement of the drug from its administration site into the systemic circulation.

mcqs.q: In a migraine, delayed oral analgesia is due to reduced gastric motility; this can be lessened by:
mcqs.explain: Metoclopramide increases gastric emptying, speeding the absorption of oral analgesics in migraine.

mcqs.q: Bioavailability is:
opts: The proportion of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation
The total amount of drug metabolised by the liver
The dose excreted unchanged in urine
The drug's affinity for its receptor
mcqs.explain: Bioavailability is the fraction of the dose reaching the systemic circulation; the area under the concentration-time curve reflects the total amount absorbed.

mcqs.q: Bioavailability of an orally administered drug is directly related to its:
opts: Solubility in body fluids (poor solubility = low bioavailability)
mcqs.explain: Oral bioavailability depends on solubility; poorly soluble drugs are poorly absorbed and have low bioavailability.

mcqs.q: The first-pass effect refers to:
opts: Hepatic metabolism of a GI-absorbed drug before it reaches the systemic circulation
The first dose of a drug a patient takes
mcqs.explain: Drugs absorbed from the gut pass via the hepatic portal vein to the liver, which metabolises part of the dose (first-pass) before systemic circulation.

mcqs.q: Which drug undergoes substantial first-pass metabolism?
mcqs.explain: Propranolol, salbutamol (oral) and verapamil undergo substantial first-pass metabolism, reducing oral bioavailability.

mcqs.q: Glyceryl trinitrate cannot be given orally and is taken sublingually because:
opts: Its first-pass breakdown in the liver is complete
It is too large to swallow
mcqs.explain: Glyceryl trinitrate is completely destroyed by first-pass metabolism, so it must bypass the liver via the sublingual route.

mcqs.q: Drugs bound to plasma proteins (e.g. albumin) are:
opts: Pharmacologically inactive, because the complex cannot cross cell membranes
mcqs.explain: The protein-bound fraction is inactive — only free (unbound) drug can cross membranes and reach its target.

mcqs.q: Which plasma protein is the major drug-binding protein?
mcqs.explain: Albumin is the main plasma protein that binds drugs; low albumin increases the free (active) fraction.

mcqs.q: A patient with LOW albumin (e.g. in some heart, circulation or diabetes conditions) will have:
mcqs.explain: Less albumin means less binding, so more free (active) drug — important in polypharmacy and dose adjustment.

mcqs.q: Besides protein binding, distribution also depends on:
opts: Cardiac output and regional blood flow
mcqs.explain: Distribution is influenced by cardiac output, regional blood flow and plasma-protein binding.

mcqs.q: Why are most emergency medications given intravenously?
opts: To avoid drug degradation in the liver and act immediately
Because IV is the slowest route
Because oral is unavailable for all drugs
mcqs.explain: IV delivery bypasses hepatic first-pass degradation and gives an immediate, 100%-bioavailable effect — ideal in emergencies.

mcqs.q: Which drugs are better taken WITH food to reduce gastric irritation?
mcqs.explain: Metformin and levodopa irritate an empty stomach, so they are better taken with food; food can also slow some drugs (e.g. fatty food slows sildenafil).

mcqs.q: The area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) represents:
opts: The total amount of drug absorbed
mcqs.explain: The AUC of the concentration-time curve reflects the total amount of drug that has been absorbed into the circulation.

mcqs.q: Pharmacodynamics describes:
opts: What the drug does to the body, including its molecular mechanism
What the body does to the drug
How a drug is excreted only
mcqs.explain: Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body — its effects and molecular mechanism of action.

saqs.a: Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug (ADME). Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body (its mechanism/effect).

saqs.q: Classify routes of administration with examples.
saqs.a: Enteral (via GIT): oral, sublingual, buccal, rectal. Parenteral (bypass GIT): IV, IM, SC, inhalation, topical.

saqs.q: Define bioavailability and state it for the IV route.
saqs.a: The proportion of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation. IV bioavailability = 100% (direct into blood).

saqs.q: Explain the first-pass effect and give a drug that must avoid it.
saqs.a: GI-absorbed drugs pass via the hepatic portal vein to the liver, which metabolises part of the dose so only a fraction reaches circulation. Glyceryl trinitrate is fully destroyed first-pass, so it is given sublingually.

saqs.q: How does plasma-protein binding affect drug activity?
saqs.a: Drug bound to albumin is pharmacologically inactive (cannot cross membranes); only the free fraction is active. Low albumin raises the free, active fraction.

saqs.q: List four factors that affect drug absorption.
saqs.a: Dosage form, presence of food, GI pH, mesenteric blood flow (and concurrent drugs / GI contents).

saqs.q: Why are most emergency drugs given IV?
saqs.a: IV gives 100% bioavailability, an immediate effect, and avoids hepatic first-pass degradation.
